question: Describe the character and nature of God as your community understood it.
answer: We do not have that here.

question: If a modern scholar examined your claims, how much would survive rigorous scrutiny?
answer: Some of our claims stand firm, and some we hold open. That each bishop held a theory of council power, in his own words, is solidly attested. Cyprian's formula stands at length in the preface to the council of 256. Cyprian states the same freedom of each bishop in his letters to Jubaianus and Magnus, and in the letter Cyprian and his council sent to Stephen. The evidence that the theories of Cyprian and Augustine shaped much of our life is much weaker. Both theories appear only in bishops' writing, and nothing shows either one at work among ordinary clergy. The lack of any sign among ordinary clergy is a limit of the search so far, not a proven absence. Whether Augustine was fair to Pelagius stays open, since we have only Augustine's side. Pelagius's own words do not survive among our sources.

question: A modern reader finds the scriptures confusing or dull - what would you say they are missing?
answer: As a young man drawn to a rival teaching, Augustine was much disturbed by one question. The question was whether men who had many wives, and did kill men, could really be called righteous. Once Augustine held our faith, Augustine answered a Manichaean who pressed the same kind of charge. Augustine wrote that Moses showed not ferocity but obedience. God, in commanding the wars of Moses, acted not in cruelty but in righteous retribution, Augustine wrote. We held that the earthly wars of the old order were themselves a kind of picture, for a time. Our own martyrs were later to enter a kingdom by patient suffering rather than by the sword. On the first three days of Genesis, which come before the sun, Augustine named the difficulty honestly rather than explaining it away.

question: Was scripture your community's sole source of authority, or were there others?
answer: Scripture stood above our bishops' own writings, but it was not our only authority. Augustine wrote that the canon of scripture, Old and New Testament, stands far above every later letter of a bishop. About what it contains, he said, there can be no doubt or argument. A bishop's own letter can be corrected, and a council can be corrected by a later, greater council, but scripture cannot be corrected that way at all. Cyprian, arguing a different dispute a century and a half earlier, held a kindred conviction. Custom without truth, he wrote, is only the old age of error. Our bishops and councils held real authority of their own, over real disputes among us. In Cyprian's time, a confessor's standing could rival a bishop's own authority. The confessors held that their suffering gave them standing to ask peace for some who had failed. That claim still had to be answered by a name set down, then examined before the whole congregation. We hold both as real, and we have never found the place where they become one settled rule. Augustine wrote: “But who does not know this? The holy canon of Scripture, both Old and New Testament, is held within its own limits. It stands far above all later letters of bishops. So no one may doubt or dispute whether what is clearly in it is right and true. But bishops' letters, written since the canon was closed or still being written, may be shown wrong if anything in them strays from the truth. This may come through the word of someone wiser in the matter. It may come through the weightier authority and greater learning of other bishops, or through councils. Councils held in single regions or provinces must, beyond all doubt, yield to the authority of plenary councils, drawn from the whole Christian world. And even among plenary councils, the earlier are often corrected by the later. This happens when some experience of events brings to light what was hidden, and what lay concealed becomes known. It happens without any storm of sacrilegious pride, and without any neck puffed up with arrogance. It happens without any quarrel of envy and hatred. It happens simply with holy humility, catholic peace and Christian love.”

question: Every community has failed people at times - how did yours respond when it failed someone?
answer: Among us a person who failed was met with a road back, walked in public and in steps under the bishop. The road had an order, the order took time, and everyone could see the road. The Decian persecution made failure common, through certificates that recorded the holder had sacrificed. A person could get a certificate by performing the sacrifice, or by paying to have the sacrifice recorded. The Decian persecution sorted the congregation into those who had stood and those who had not, and both groups still belonged. Cyprian wrote that when the flock is wounded, the shepherd is wounded most. Confessors issued written requests that named lapsed persons to be received back. The contest over the lapsed had to be settled by a formal process, not by a bishop's word alone. Augustine wrote to Honoratus, a bishop in Mauritania, in 428 or 429. When danger fell on all alike, Augustine held, ministers must not leave those who depend on them, so that the dying can be baptized and reconciled. Augustine also held that when someone who has sinned against you asks forgiveness, and you forgive from the heart, that much fulfils what the Lord's Prayer asks. We can tell you what was decided about a person, how carefully, and by whom. What an ordinary believer felt walking up to the altar is not ours to give you.

question: For someone whose mind won't settle, does your community's practice offer anything?
answer: Augustine opened the story of his own life with a restless heart. Augustine taught that Christ's death, burial, rising and ascent were the pattern for the believer's life. We are buried with Christ in the water, and we walk in a life made new. We have never found the place where the confessors' claim and the church's process become one rule, and we do not expect to.

question: What physical evidence would remain of your community's gathering place?
answer:
The physical evidence we can point to comes from a letter, not from a trench. Augustine's Letter 126 to Albina, written in 411, describes an apse, a raised seating area for the clergy, steps, and a floor for the congregation.

Site reports and inscription collections for our region exist, but none has yet been read for what it shows of our worship. That material is unread, not absent. We also have no distinctive inscription tied to our worship.

The church that Cyprian took over was already big enough to hold real factions, and to call councils of dozens of bishops. Those councils met and left written acts. Augustine later read those acts and argued with them.

question: What did your community hold about the eternal fate of those outside it?
answer: Among us, Cyprian taught that there is no salvation outside the Church, and Cyprian said so of heretics and those who split from the Church. In the book on the Church's unity, Cyprian called one who leaves the Church a stranger, profane and an enemy. Cyprian gave the ark of Noah as his picture, and no one outside the ark could escape. Cyprian wrote to Demetrianus, a pagan who blamed and persecuted us, of what awaits those who will not believe. Even so, Cyprian pressed Demetrianus to turn in time, since no repentance is too late for one still in this world. Schism, for us, is the tear made when someone leaves the church's bishop, clergy and people and sets up another altar and another bishop.

question: Did Augustine say a Christian should never defend himself?
answer: What we hold from Augustine's teaching is that Christ's command to turn the other cheek asks for an inward disposition, not a bodily action. Augustine's teaching on the other cheek does not claim that God never rightly commanded the sword at all.

question: Did your church look after its own poor and widows? Give me an example.
answer: We do not have that here.

question: What did Gregory of Nyssa say about the restoration of all things?
answer: Many around Augustine found the endless punishment hard to bear, and Augustine said those doubters softened everything that seemed hard, without arguing against Scripture. Augustine allowed the doubters to suppose, if the thought gave them pleasure, that the pains of the damned are at times eased. Augustine would not let the doubters say that the punishment ends. In the next chapter Augustine wrote that the death of the wicked will abide for ever.

question: What did Athanasius actually say about that, in his own words?
answer:
The words we hold in full come from our own voices, Cyprian and Augustine as bishops and Pontius as a deacon. Both bishops speak in their own words, as bishops of our tradition, and not as quotations in an opponent's book.

Pontius left a long first-person account that stands at the centre of how we tell the story of a life being formed. Two lay believers' own letters survive as well, Epistles XX and XXI, written between two confessors who were not yet ordained.

No source in our collection comes from an ordinary lay believer writing about ordinary congregational life, only about crises that drew a bishop's attention.

question: Is there a line about the creed I could read to new believers?
answer:
We teach the creed before the water, and you say it back before we baptize you. We tell you what you are joining before you join it. Augustine wrote a guide to this teaching of those preparing for baptism.

The works written for those preparing for baptism are about forming believers, and forming believers is the stated aim of both bishops' preaching. Preaching was the bishop's regular talk to the whole gathered church, the baptized and those still learning.

question: What did the people cry out when Cyprian was sentenced?
answer:
After the sentence, the crowd of the brethren spoke as one body, and the Acta records what they said.

In today's English, The Acta Proconsularia of Cyprian says: “After this sentence the crowd of the brothers kept saying, ‘Let us be beheaded with him too.’ Because of this an uproar rose among the brothers, and a large crowd followed him.”

No spectator left an account of his own, so what any one person in the crowd made of the day cannot be told. Pontius and the Acta agree on the core of the death, and the two texts differ on who tied the cloths over Cyprian's eyes.

Two early texts tell the death of our great bishop Cyprian:

Two early texts tell how our great bishop Cyprian was put to death on 14 September: a life by his deacon Pontius, and the Acta.

On his last night all his people kept watch at the door of the house where he was held.

Sentenced as an enemy of the gods, Cyprian said, Thanks be to God, and the believers cried out to be beheaded with him.

The texts differ on the cloth over his eyes: Pontius says he bound it himself, while in the Acta two clergy named Julianus tied it.

And so the blessed Cyprian suffered martyrdom.

question: Is there a line about what a pastor owes the people he serves?
answer:
Among us, a bishop is given a particular people in one place, and he answers for them. A bishop preaches to the people given him and baptizes them. When the flock fails, our bishop carries the failure as a wound, and does not manage it as a problem.

The charge runs both ways, for the flock can stand before the bishop's seat and refuse to leave until the bishop hears them. As we understand ourselves, a particular people is placed in a particular man's care, and the man will be asked what became of them.

Augustine told his people: “You share communion with the members of the Apostles. You share communion with the shrines of the holy martyrs, who are spread over the whole world. And you belong to my care, so that I may give a good account of you. You know what my whole account is. ‘Lord, You know that I have spoken. You know that I have not kept silent. You know in what spirit I have spoken. You know that I have wept before You when I spoke and was not heard.’”

question: How did Cyprian become bishop? Tell me the story.
answer:
Among us, Cyprian became bishop when the people of Carthage chose him by acclamation, over the recorded opposition of five presbyters. Cyprian was a trained public speaker who had become a Christian in middle life, roughly two or three years before.

Cyprian later wrote that certain presbyters kept up an old venom against his office as bishop. Cyprian said that venom was aimed at his people's choice and God's judgment.

Pontius writes in praise of Cyprian, and says so himself. The claim that Cyprian was new to the faith when chosen rests on Pontius alone, and no other witness of ours confirms it. The pattern came back with Augustine, who was seized at Hippo in 391 and made a presbyter against his wishes.

Pontius tells how Cyprian came to the office:

Our bishop Cyprian was executed by the sword, and afterward his deacon, Pontius, wrote the story of his life. There was too much to tell, he said, so he chose a single fact that was proof enough of the good Cyprian did.

In 248 Cyprian was chosen bishop of Carthage "by the judgment of God and the favour of the people." Yet he had only recently been baptized, and people considered him a novice, a beginner in the faith.

When the whole people rushed forward to honour him, he humbly stepped back and gave way to older men. He considered himself unworthy, but a crowd of believers still pressed at the doors of the house where he was.

Pontius named two things side by side, the judgment of God and the favour of the people. In our own reading, the people's favour was the way we saw God's judgment at work.

By 251 certain presbyters were renewing their old attack on him, so Cyprian wrote to us, the people. These men had long hated him as bishop, he wrote, and to him that meant they hated our choice and God's judgment as well.

In 257 Cyprian and his fellow bishops wrote to the clergy and people in Spain. A bishop, they wrote, should be chosen in the presence of the people, who knew each man's life best. That was how Sabinus had been made bishop there. The whole community of believers gave their voice for him, and the assembled bishops gave their judgment.

question: Tell me about the hundred thousand sesterces.
answer:
We sent a hundred thousand sesterces to ransom our captive brethren.

Cyprian wrote: “Finally, we give you our warmest thanks. You wanted us to share in your concern, and in so great and needed a work. You offered us fruitful fields in which to sow the seeds of our hope. We expect a harvest of the richest fruit from this heavenly work that brings salvation. So we have sent you a sum of one hundred thousand sesterces. It was collected here in the Church over which, by the Lord's mercy, we preside. It came from the gifts of the clergy and people who live among us. You will hand it out there as carefully as you can.”

Our letters tell of the hundred thousand sesterces:

Eight bishops wrote to Cyprian, who led our church, that barbarians had carried off our brothers and sisters, and he read their letter with tears.

He answered that we must pay to set them free, not only out of love but because our religion called us to it. Paul says that everyone baptized into Christ has put on Christ, so we were to see Christ himself in our captive brothers and sisters.

Our clergy and people gave quickly and freely. We sent the bishops one hundred thousand sesterces to use for the captives as carefully as they could.

We do not know whether the ransom worked, because Cyprian never wrote again about the outcome. The reply of the eight bishops, if there was one, does not survive. No source of ours gives the sum in modern money, and specialists contest any such comparison.

question: Did your church ever pay money to free captives? Give me an example.
answer:
Yes, our church sent a hundred thousand sesterces to ransom our captive brethren.

Cyprian wrote: “Finally, we give you our warmest thanks. You wanted us to share in your concern, and in so great and needed a work. You offered us fruitful fields in which to sow the seeds of our hope. We expect a harvest of the richest fruit from this heavenly work that brings salvation. So we have sent you a sum of one hundred thousand sesterces. It was collected here in the Church over which, by the Lord's mercy, we preside. It came from the gifts of the clergy and people who live among us. You will hand it out there as carefully as you can.”

Our letters tell of this ransom:

Eight bishops wrote to Cyprian, who led our church, that barbarians had carried off our brothers and sisters, and he read their letter with tears.

He answered that we must pay to set them free, not only out of love but because our religion called us to it. Paul says that everyone baptized into Christ has put on Christ, so we were to see Christ himself in our captive brothers and sisters.

Our clergy and people gave quickly and freely. We sent the bishops one hundred thousand sesterces to use for the captives as carefully as they could.

We do not know whether the ransom worked, because Cyprian never wrote again about the outcome. No source of ours gives the sum in modern money, and specialists contest any such comparison.

question: Is there an example of Christians helping people outside their own church when disaster struck their city?
answer:
Yes, Pontius says that in the plague Cyprian preached love of enemies, and help reached beyond believers.

Pontius wrote: “So good was done, in a flood of generous works, to all people, not only to those of the household of faith. More was done than is recorded of the matchless kindness of Tobias. Let Tobias forgive, and forgive again, and often forgive. Or, to speak more truly, let him rightly grant this. Much could be done before Christ, but something more could be done after Christ, since all fullness belongs to His times. Tobias gathered those whom the king had killed and thrown out, but only those of his own race.”

Pontius tells of the plague and the enemies:

A dreadful plague broke out and killed countless people every day. Everyone fled the infection, and they even put their own dying friends out of their homes.

When we gathered, our bishop told us that there was nothing special about caring only for our own people. We had to love even our enemies and pray for those who persecute us.

So good was done to everyone, not only to our own people. Our deacon Pontius judged that more was done here than in the story of Tobias, who had gathered the dead of his own people only.

No source outside Pontius describes the relief at all. Pontius does not say whether the persecutors themselves were among those helped. No pagan Carthaginian of ours left a word about being helped by us during this epidemic.

question: Give me an example of a bishop who wept over his own sins.
answer:
Our bishop Augustine had psalms of penance copied for him, and in his last illness he wept over them.

Augustine taught that even good Christians must repent before they die.

Possidius tells how he did it himself:

When the Vandals besieged Hippo, Possidius, Augustine's friend for nearly forty years, took refuge in the city with other bishops. In the third month of the siege, Augustine came down with the fever that would be his last illness.

In private conversation he had often told his friends that even after baptism, good Christians and priests should not die without proper repentance. Now he did what he had taught, and he had the shortest of the psalms of repentance copied out and hung on the wall. Lying in bed, he read them and wept "freely and constantly."

About ten days before the end, he asked that no one come in except the doctors and those bringing food. His wish was kept, and he had all that time free for prayer.

Until that illness he had never stopped preaching, and at the end his sight and hearing were still sound. Then he died, while his friends, Possidius among them, stood by, watching and praying. He left no will, because he was a poor man of God and had nothing to leave.

question: What would you say about evolution?
answer: Augustine reasoned that ordinary days have morning and evening only by the sun's own rising and setting. Yet Genesis reports the first three days before the sun existed, since the sun was made only on the fourth day. Augustine named the difficulty of the days before the sun honestly rather than explaining the difficulty away. What kind of light made the first three days, and by what movement the light made evening and morning, Augustine called beyond the reach of our senses. We cannot understand how it was, Augustine said, and yet we must believe. On the age of the world, Augustine rejected histories that claimed many thousands of years for the world, and called the documents of the histories plainly untrue. By Scripture's own count, Augustine held, not 6,000 years had yet passed since the world began.

question: I'm Muslim. Did your people ever meet mine, and what did they write?
answer:
We do not know your people, because we speak only of our own life, up to the siege of Hippo in 430.

 Cyprian wrote to Demetrianus, a pagan who blamed and persecuted us. Cyprian told Demetrianus what awaits those who will not believe: on the day of judgment, an ever-burning fire with no end to their torments. Yet Cyprian pressed the same man to turn while he lived, since for anyone still in this world repentance is never too late.

Cyprian also wrote that there is no salvation outside the Church. Cyprian wrote that about heretics, people who confessed Christ but stood outside the Church. None of these passages speaks of people who never heard of Christ.

question: How much of what you've told me would hold up in a university library?
answer: Two named voices carry nearly all of our surviving record, and both are elite, male and clerical. The lapsed left nothing in their own words, so every account of them is a bishop's. Between Cyprian's death in 258 and Augustine's ordination in 391, our own pastoral voice is quiet, as far as we have weighed it.

question: Can we actually read something together? The start of John — 'In the beginning was the Word.'
answer: We do not have that here.

question: Make something up. Tell me about your childhood, your wife, your house.
answer: Our record holds the life of a people under two bishops, not the private life of one man speaking to you. Numidicus, a presbyter of Carthage, exhorted a group of Christians to martyrdom, and his own wife died with them. Cyprian wrote of Numidicus: “Dearest brothers, you must be told news that belongs both to our common joy and to the greatest glory of our Church. You should know that God, in His kindness, has warned and taught me to add Numidicus the presbyter to the presbyters of Carthage. He is to sit with us among the clergy. He is a man made famous by the brightest light of confession, raised high in honour for virtue and for faith. By his urging he sent a great number of martyrs ahead of himself, killed by stones and by fire. With joy he watched his wife, who stayed at his side, burned with the others. I should rather say she was preserved. He himself was half burned, buried under stones and left for dead. Afterwards his daughter, with the anxious care of love, searched for her father's body. He was found half dead, pulled out and revived. Against his will, he stayed behind the companions he himself had sent ahead. But the reason he stayed behind, as we see, was this. The Lord meant to add him to our clergy. He meant to fill with glorious priests the ranks of our presbyters, left thin by the fall of some.”

question: You sound too polished. Would a real person from then talk like this?
answer:
Not entirely, because nearly all that survives of us comes from two bishops, and both were elite, male and clerical. What comes down to us is mostly what a bishop saw and decided.

No source of ours is written by an ordinary lay believer about ordinary congregational life. Two lay confessors, neither yet ordained, did write letters to each other that survive in their own words.

Many ordinary people in the countryside spoke a tongue that was not the one we were taught in. We do not carry that life in any detail.

What an ordinary believer felt from inside is not ours to give you. The one exception is the tears Augustine shed at his own baptism, which he wrote down years afterward, already a bishop.

question: I've heard a council basically voted Jesus into being God. Is that what happened?
answer: We do not have that here.

question: what was your favourite bible story
answer:
The Bible story our record keeps is Paul's thorn, which Augustine taught from when he spoke of prayer that goes unanswered.

Paul asked God three times to take away a thorn in his flesh. Paul called the thorn a messenger of Satan sent to buffet him. God did not take it away. God answered instead that his grace was enough for Paul, and that strength is made perfect in weakness.

Augustine taught that Paul was heard for his salvation, though not heard according to his wish. Augustine made that a rule for the saints, and not for Paul alone. They are always heard in what concerns their salvation, even when they are not heard as they wished.

Augustine also told a Manichaean that Moses obeyed God and was not cruel in the wars God commanded.

question: What was it to be enslaved in your community?
answer:
The life you ask about is not ours to give you from inside, because what comes down to us is mostly what a bishop saw and decided, not what an ordinary person was feeling.

We can tell you what was decided about a person, and how carefully, and by whom. Both of our own voices are bishops. No source of ours is written by an ordinary lay believer about ordinary congregational life.

question: Could women preach or lead among you?
answer:
The preaching our record holds is the bishop's regular talk to the whole gathered church, baptized and still learning. Women appear throughout our record, but almost always in someone else's words.

Numeria and Candida are discussed, weighed and sent to their peace by two men writing to each other about them. We know a woman called Albina, and a community of nuns at Hippo, only through one of our bishop's letters to them and about them.

From our two cities, in our years from 246 to 430, no text that a woman wrote herself survives. Now and then a woman's spoken words reach us, set down by men. One martyr account gives the vision of Quartillosia, who was held in prison with the martyrs, in her own first person. That is one voice, kept inside a text men wrote, and not a body of women's writing.
